Find rows that repeat a key, and choose which to keep

Source: R/duplicate_keys.R
duplicate_keys.Rd

Lists the rows of data that share a value of key, such as a patient with two operations on the same day under the key c("ccfid", "dt_surg"). Given order_by, it also marks the first row of each repeated key to keep, which is how the SAS jobs resolve them: the first operation is kept and the second is treated as a complication of it.

Usage

duplicate_keys(data, key, order_by = NULL, show_key = FALSE)

Arguments

data

A data frame.

key

Names of the columns that should make each row unique.

order_by

NULL (the default), or names of the columns that order the rows of a repeated key. Required for keep.

show_key

Include the key columns in rows? Default FALSE.

Value

An object of class duplicate_keys, a list of three:

summary

One row: rows, keys (distinct key values), repeated_keys, rows_in_repeats and missing_keys (rows missing any key column).

rows

One row per row of data in a repeated key, in data order: row, its row number in data; .group, numbering the repeated keys in order of appearance; .rank, its place within the key by order_by (NA without order_by); then the key columns when show_key = TRUE.

keep

A logical vector, one per row of data: TRUE for every row outside a repeated key and for the first row of each repeated key. NULL without order_by.

Details

data is never changed. Subset it with keep: data[dk$keep, ] is unique on key, and data[!dk$keep, ] holds the rows set aside, to record or to carry as complications. Drop rows in the build, where corrections belong, not in a study job.

"First" means first when the rows of a repeated key are sorted by the order_by columns, in ascending order. When the first two rows of a repeated key tie on order_by, or a row in a repeated key is missing an order_by value, there is no first row to keep, and the function stops rather than pick one. Add a column that separates them, such as the time of the operation.

A missing key value is treated as a value, as duplicated treats it, so two rows missing the key repeat it. Missing keys are also counted in summary.

Key values are left out of rows unless show_key = TRUE, because a key is usually a patient identifier. Use rows$row to look at the rows in data.

See also

register_data, whose key argument refuses a dataset that repeats it.

Examples

ops <- data.frame(
  id = c(1, 2, 2, 3),
  dt_surg = as.Date(c("2010-01-05", "2012-03-01", "2012-03-01", "2011-06-01")),
  op_time = c(8, 14, 9, 10)
)
dk <- duplicate_keys(ops, c("id", "dt_surg"), order_by = "op_time")
dk
#> Key: id, dt_surg
#> 4 rows, 3 distinct keys. 1 key repeats, over 2 rows.
#> Keeping the first by op_time: 1 rows set aside.
dk$rows
#>   row .group .rank
#> 1   2      1     2
#> 2   3      1     1
ops[dk$keep, ]
#>   id    dt_surg op_time
#> 1  1 2010-01-05       8
#> 3  2 2012-03-01       9
#> 4  3 2011-06-01      10
ops[!dk$keep, ]
#>   id    dt_surg op_time
#> 2  2 2012-03-01      14
